books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Utopian Communities

stimulus.text: The photograph shows the Oneida Community in New York in the 1860s and 1870s: a large brick communal building with a tower, set on open grounds where small groups of people walk and gather. The Oneida Community was founded in 1848 by John Humphrey Noyes as a utopian community in which members shared property and labor and practiced complex marriage, the sharing of spouses within the community.
stimulus.source_note: Description records only what the photograph visibly shows; the facts about Oneida's founding, Noyes, shared property, and complex marriage come from Princeton Review, Chapter 8, and the standard account of the community. Photograph: Oneida Commune, c. 1865-1875, by Moulton and Dopp, public domain; image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus describes a public-domain photograph of the Oneida Community (c. 1865-1875)
stem: The photograph most directly illustrates which of the following features of antebellum utopian communities?

options.text: Members lived alone in cabins scattered through the wilderness
options.misconception: Thoreau lived alone in a cabin, so a utopian community can look like solitary cabins in the woods.

options.text: Members lived together in one large building and shared property and labor
Members worked in factories owned by outside investors for cash wages
options.misconception: Factories and wages were the era's economy, so a community can look like a factory town.

options.text: Members built walled forts to defend themselves against the federal army
options.misconception: Communities that broke the rules can look like forts, and the army fought in the West then.

rationales.A: The photograph shows one large building housing the community, not scattered solitary cabins. Thoreau's cabin was a different experiment.
rationales.B: The big brick building with shared grounds is communal living made visible: one home, shared property, shared labor.
rationales.C: Oneida shared property and labor among its own members; it was not a factory town paying cash wages to workers for outside investors.
rationales.D: No walls, forts, or soldiers appear. Oneida was a peaceful community, not a fort defending itself against the army.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the building: one large brick home with a tower, not separate houses.
2. Look at the grounds: open lawns where members walk and gather together.
3. Name the pattern: communal living, where property and labor are shared by the whole group.
Background: John Humphrey Noyes founded Oneida in 1848; members also practiced complex marriage.
Remember: the building is the belief, and one big house means one shared life.

figures.caption: The Oneida Community in New York, photographed about 1865-1875. Members shared one large home.
figures.alt: An 1860s photograph of the Oneida Community's large brick communal building with a tower, set on open grounds with people walking
